paragraphs: Convert SRT subtitle files to WebVTT format instantly. Paste or upload your .srt file and download a ready-to-use .vtt file. Free, no account, runs in your browser.

Upload the video or paste a public URL. Word-level timestamp alignment produces more accurate line breaks than sentence-level alignment — each subtitle break falls at a natural pause rather than a word boundary mid-phrase.

Flag any line above 17 CPS and split it. An 8-word subtitle in a 1.2-second window hits approximately 24 CPS — unreadable for most viewers. Merge subtitle lines shorter than 0.8 seconds, which display too briefly to register.

Subtitle overlap — where the next block starts before the previous one ends — causes display flicker in most players. Any gap shorter than 0.1 seconds between adjacent subtitles should be merged or widened to prevent rendering artifacts.

Export SRT for YouTube, Vimeo, and video editors. Export VTT for HTML5 web players and streaming platforms that support caption positioning. Choose burned-caption output for Instagram Reels, TikTok clips, and any social context where autoplay without sound is expected.

Standard timed subtitle format: sequence number, timestamp pair (00:00:00,000 → 00:00:00,000 with comma separator), and one or two lines of caption text per block. Supported by YouTube, Vimeo, LinkedIn, most video editors, and accessibility workflows.

WebVTT format with period timestamp separators (00:00:00.000 → 00:00:00.000). Used by HTML5 video players, streaming services, and accessibility platforms. Unlike SRT, VTT supports <cue> positioning metadata, text styling, and karaoke-mode highlighting.

Permanently embedded caption text rendered directly into the video frame — cannot be toggled off by the viewer. Required for platforms that strip external caption tracks. Font rendering, shadow depth, and vertical position all need QA review after encoding because video compression can degrade caption legibility.
Generate SRT for YouTube upload, export burned captions for Instagram Reels, and produce VTT for course platform embeds — all from the same subtitle pass without reformatting timing.
Produce synchronized captions that meet WCAG 2.1 timing and reading-speed requirements. CPS validation catches lines that fail accessibility guidelines before the video goes live.
Export SRT or VTT for import into Premiere, DaVinci Resolve, or Final Cut Pro. Accurate word-level timestamps eliminate the need to manually re-sync caption timing after import.

Eight words spoken in 1.2 seconds: "we need to fix this before the deadline" at 24 CPS. The line must be split into two display segments within the same timing window to hit the readable 14–17 CPS range.
Block ending at 00:01:23,500 overlapping a block starting at 00:01:23,200 causes display flicker and rendering failure in most SRT players. A subtitle validator catches this before upload.

A two-line subtitle with 44+ characters per line at default font sizes clips at the bottom of mobile video frames. The safe area for mobile subtitles is a single line, 38 characters maximum, positioned at 85% vertical height.

Font stroke weight, drop shadow depth, and subtitle vertical position all shift slightly after H.264 encoding. Captions that look correct in preview may become harder to read in the encoded file — requires a post-encode QA pass before publishing.

UTF-8 encoding required. Maximum 1,500 subtitle blocks per file. Timestamp format: 00:00:00,000 (comma separator, not period). Files over 1,500 blocks need splitting before upload. YouTube auto-syncs uploaded SRT to audio — small timing offsets are corrected automatically.

TikTok generates its own auto-captions and displays them over uploaded SRT files in most cases. Burned captions are the reliable method for ensuring accurate captions appear on TikTok content. SRT upload works but TikTok may override it.

Instagram does not display soft subtitle tracks during autoplay in Feed or Reels. Burned captions are the only reliable method for ensuring captions appear for silent autoplay viewers. Instagram's built-in auto-caption feature can also be used after upload, but accuracy varies.

VTT uses period timestamp separators (00:00:00.000) while SRT uses commas (00:00:00,000). Swapping the separator character breaks parsing in most players. VTT files must begin with the WEBVTT header line — SRT files must not.

CPS stands for characters per second — how fast the viewer must read a subtitle line before it disappears. The readable range is 14–17 CPS for most general audiences. Above 21 CPS, a significant percentage of viewers cannot finish reading the line before it vanishes, even if the text is accurate. Most automated subtitle tools generate lines without a CPS check, which is why reviewing reading speed is part of subtitle QA before any platform upload.

Instagram Reels does not display soft subtitle tracks during autoplay in Feed. External SRT or VTT files uploaded to Instagram are not surfaced for most viewers. For Reels content, burned (hardcoded) captions are the only reliable method for ensuring captions appear — either by using a burn workflow before upload or using Instagram's built-in auto-caption feature after upload, which has variable accuracy.

Video encoding (particularly H.264 and H.265) applies compression that slightly degrades text edges. Font stroke weight, drop shadow contrast, and subtitle position all shift after encoding. Captions that look clean in an editing preview may develop legibility issues in the exported file. A post-encode QA pass — watching 2–3 minutes of the encoded video at actual playback size — should be part of any burned caption workflow before the file is published.

SRT uses comma separators in timestamps: 00:01:23,456 → 00:01:25,123. VTT uses period separators: 00:01:23.456 → 00:01:25.123. Swapping the separator character causes parsing failures in most players — the file appears empty or throws an error. SRT files must not begin with a header; VTT files must begin with the line "WEBVTT". The two formats are otherwise structurally similar but not interchangeable.

Progressive timing drift — where captions start slightly late early in the video and progressively fall further behind — usually indicates an audio-video sync issue in the source file, not a transcription error. The subtitle timestamps were generated against audio that does not match the video track timing. Fix: use the subtitle timing fixer to shift all timestamps by the measured offset at a known sync point early in the video. If the drift accelerates over time, the source file has a variable frame rate issue that requires frame-rate normalization before re-captioning.

VideoText exports SRT and VTT subtitle files. SRT works with YouTube, Vimeo, LinkedIn, and most video editors. VTT is the standard for HTML5 web players and streaming platforms — it also supports styling and positioning metadata that SRT does not carry. Burned caption output is available for social clips that require permanently embedded text. All exports are UTF-8 encoded.

VTT uses period timestamp separators (00:00:00.000) while SRT uses commas (00:00:00,000). Swapping the separator character breaks parsing in most players. VTT files must begin with the WEBVTT header line — SRT files must not.

CPS stands for characters per second — how fast the viewer must read a subtitle line before it disappears. The readable range is 14–17 CPS for most general audiences. The subtitle timestamps were generated against audio that does not match the video track timing. Fix: use the subtitle timing fixer to shift all timestamps by the measured offset at a known sync point early in the video. If the drift accelerates over time, the source file has a variable frame rate issue that requires frame-rate normalization before re-captioning.

For Reels content, burned (hardcoded) captions are the only reliable method for ensuring captions appear — either by using a burn workflow before upload or using Instagram's built-in auto-caption feature after upload, which has variable accuracy.

Video encoding (particularly H.264 and H.265) applies compression that slightly degrades text edges. Font stroke weight, drop shadow contrast, and subtitle position all shift after encoding. SRT uses comma separators in timestamps: 00:01:23,456 → 00:01:25,123. VTT uses period separators: 00:01:23.456 → 00:01:25.123. Swapping the separator character causes parsing failures in most players — the file appears empty or throws an error. SRT files must not begin with a header; VTT files must begin with the line "WEBVTT". The two formats are otherwise structurally similar but not interchangeable.

Progressive timing drift — where captions start slightly late early in the video and progressively fall further behind — usually indicates an audio-video sync issue in the source file, not a transcription error. The subtitle timestamps were generated against audio that does not match the video track timing. Fix: use the subtitle timing fixer to shift all timestamps by the measured offset at a known sync point early in the video. If the drift accelerates over time, the source file has a variable frame rate issue that requires frame-rate normalization before re-captioning.

paragraphs: The TranscribeMe qualification exam tests intelligent verbatim — the hardest part for new transcribers. This guide covers what the exam evaluates, the most common failure reasons, and how to prepare effectively.

Choose Rev, GoTranscript, TranscribeMe, Scribie, or a custom client specification. Each guideline has distinct rules for verbatim level, speaker label format, timestamp intervals, inaudible notation, and maximum paragraph length.

Clean verbatim removes fillers, false starts, and repetitions for readability. Full verbatim preserves all spoken content. Applying the wrong level is the most common single reason transcripts fail marketplace QA — it cannot be fixed without re-reading the source audio.

A single speaker must have exactly one label format from the first occurrence to the last. Mixed formats (JOHN SMITH / John / J. Smith) require a find-and-replace pass across the full document before any other formatting work.

Rev-style: timestamps every 2 minutes or at each speaker change. GoTranscript: no timestamp requirement by default. TranscribeMe: per-speaker-turn timestamps. Paragraph length limits range from 8 lines (Rev) to no limit (some custom clients).

Verify inaudible notation consistency (all [inaudible] or all [INAUDIBLE], never mixed), check bracket format for crosstalk sections, confirm verbatim level is consistent throughout, and validate that paragraph length does not exceed the client's maximum.

Clean verbatim text. Speaker names in CAPITAL LETTERS followed by a colon. Timestamps in [HH:MM:SS] format at 2-minute intervals and at speaker changes. No paragraph longer than 8 lines. Inaudible sections marked [inaudible]. False starts and fillers removed.

Optional full or clean verbatim per client request. Speaker labels in "Speaker Name:" format with consistent capitalization. [inaudible] notation for unclear audio. No timestamp requirement unless client specifies. Paragraph breaks at topic shifts rather than fixed intervals.

Structured document with consistent heading-style speaker labels, paragraph breaks, correctly formatted timestamps, and clean or full verbatim as specified. Formatted for direct delivery — no manual cleanup required before attaching to the client email.

Reduce revision risk before submitting marketplace jobs. A pre-delivery formatting check catches the label inconsistency, timestamp format error, or verbatim level mismatch that triggers a QA rejection and unpaid revision.
Create a consistent formatting baseline across a team of transcriptionists working on the same client account — so reviewers spend time on content accuracy, not fixing label formats.

Turn raw AI-generated transcripts into readable interview documents: speaker structure, consistent punctuation, accurate paragraph breaks, and timestamps that let readers verify context in the source recording.

Page 1: "JOHN SMITH: Thanks for joining us." Page 3: "John: So as I was saying..." Page 7: "Speaker 1: Right, exactly." — All three refer to the same speaker. Label drift of this kind fails QA at every major transcript marketplace.

[00:05:12] on page 2, (00:05:12) on page 4, [5:12] on page 6, and 00:05:12 on page 8 — all in the same document. Most style guides require a single format, and inconsistency triggers automatic rejection on automated QA systems.

"[inaudible]", "[INAUDIBLE]", "[unclear]", and "[crosstalk]" appearing in the same file for the same type of audio problem. Rev requires "[inaudible]" in lowercase brackets. GoTranscript uses a different notation. Neither accepts a mix of styles.

Pages 1–4 are clean verbatim (fillers removed). Pages 5–8 switch to full verbatim (fillers preserved). This happens when an ASR tool applies different post-processing across transcript segments — and it fails QA because the verbatim level is supposed to be consistent throughout.

Clean verbatim by default. Speaker names in ALL CAPS followed by a colon. Timestamp format [HH:MM:SS] every 2 minutes and at speaker changes. Maximum paragraph: 8 lines. Inaudible: [inaudible]. Crosstalk: [crosstalk]. False starts and filler words removed.

Clean or full verbatim per client request. Speaker format "Speaker Name:" with title case. [inaudible] for unclear audio. No timestamp requirement by default (client can request). No strict paragraph length limit. Crosstalk marked with [crosstalk].

Strict verbatim — all fillers and false starts preserved. Timestamps required at each speaker turn. Speaker format "SPEAKER NAME:" in caps. Specific bracket format for technical notation. Paragraph breaks only at speaker changes.

Many agencies specify hybrid rules that don't map cleanly to any standard guide — for example, Rev-style speaker labels but GoTranscript-style verbatim and no timestamps. These combinations must be documented explicitly because the formatter cannot infer them.

The TranscribeMe test is considered moderately difficult. The main challenge is applying intelligent verbatim correctly — knowing which fillers to keep vs. remove requires judgement, not just rule-following. Candidates who have only done clean verbatim transcription often struggle with this nuance.

TranscribeMe qualification audio is typically clear, single-speaker audio of 3–5 minutes. Unlike some platforms, the test audio is chosen to be fair — it's not deliberately difficult with heavy accents or background noise. The challenge is verbatim handling, not audio quality.

TranscribeMe allows a limited number of retries. After failing, there is typically a waiting period before you can retake the test. Use this time to practice intelligent verbatim on sample audio using VideoText and the Guideline Format tool.

Focus 80% of your preparation on intelligent verbatim judgment: practice keeping meaningful fillers vs. removing habitual ones. Practice with diverse speakers — nervous, fast, casual speakers. Review speaker label format: [Name]:. Avoid ALL CAPS emphasis. Check your paragraph breaks.

Yes. TranscribeMe requires approximately 85%+ word accuracy on the test. However, formatting errors (wrong verbatim level, speaker labels, paragraph structure) can cause the transcript to fail even at high word accuracy. Both accuracy and formatting compliance are evaluated.

New paragraph for each speaker change. Within a single speaker's long turn, break paragraphs every 4–6 sentences or approximately 300 characters. Avoid very short paragraphs (single sentences) and very long ones (more than 8 sentences). Balanced paragraphs improve readability and QA scores.

[Name]: — square brackets around the name, colon after the closing bracket, then the speaker's text. For unknown speakers: [Speaker 1]:, [Speaker 2]:. Example: [Dr. Smith]: The results were encouraging.

Use an em dash (—) when a speaker is abruptly cut off or interrupted. Use an ellipsis (...) when a speaker trails off without completing their thought. Both are acceptable in TranscribeMe transcripts; the choice depends on what actually happened in the audio.
Monetary amounts use symbols and numerals: $50, €100, £250. Spell out informal references: "fifty bucks", "a hundred euros". Large round amounts: $5 million (not $5,000,000 unless precision matters).

Transcribe foreign words as spoken in the audio. If you are uncertain of the spelling, use your best judgment and mark with [?]: "The concept of schadenfreude [?] applies here." Do not translate foreign words — transcribe what was said.

Intelligent verbatim (also called smart verbatim) means you use judgement about which filler words to keep vs. remove. Keep fillers that carry meaning — e.g., "um" when it shows genuine hesitation or nervousness. Remove habitual fillers — e.g., "you know" used constantly at the end of every sentence. This is harder than clean verbatim because it requires contextual judgment.

Choose Rev, GoTranscript, TranscribeMe, Scribie, or a custom client specification. Each guideline has distinct rules for verbatim level, speaker label format, timestamp intervals, inaudible notation, and maximum paragraph length.

Clean verbatim removes fillers, false starts, and repetitions for readability. Full verbatim preserves all spoken content. Applying the wrong level is the most common single reason transcripts fail marketplace QA — it cannot be fixed without re-reading the source audio.

A single speaker must have exactly one label format from the first occurrence to the last. Mixed formats (JOHN SMITH / John / J. Smith) require a find-and-replace pass across the full document before any other formatting work.

Rev-style: timestamps every 2 minutes or at each speaker change. GoTranscript: no timestamp requirement by default. TranscribeMe: per-speaker-turn timestamps. Paragraph length limits range from 8 lines (Rev) to no limit (some custom clients).

Verify inaudible notation consistency (all [inaudible] or all [INAUDIBLE], never mixed), check bracket format for crosstalk sections, confirm verbatim level is consistent throughout, and validate that paragraph length does not exceed the client's maximum.

Clean verbatim text. Speaker names in CAPITAL LETTERS followed by a colon. Timestamps in [HH:MM:SS] format at 2-minute intervals and at speaker changes. No paragraph longer than 8 lines. Inaudible sections marked [inaudible]. False starts and fillers removed.

Optional full or clean verbatim per client request. Speaker labels in "Speaker Name:" format with consistent capitalization. [inaudible] notation for unclear audio. No timestamp requirement unless client specifies. Paragraph breaks at topic shifts rather than fixed intervals.

Structured document with consistent heading-style speaker labels, paragraph breaks, correctly formatted timestamps, and clean or full verbatim as specified. Formatted for direct delivery — no manual cleanup required before attaching to the client email.

Turn raw AI-generated transcripts into readable interview documents: speaker structure, consistent punctuation, accurate paragraph breaks, and timestamps that let readers verify context in the source recording.

Page 1: "JOHN SMITH: Thanks for joining us." Page 3: "John: So as I was saying..." Page 7: "Speaker 1: Right, exactly." — All three refer to the same speaker. Label drift of this kind fails QA at every major transcript marketplace.

[00:05:12] on page 2, (00:05:12) on page 4, [5:12] on page 6, and 00:05:12 on page 8 — all in the same document. Most style guides require a single format, and inconsistency triggers automatic rejection on automated QA systems.

"[inaudible]", "[INAUDIBLE]", "[unclear]", and "[crosstalk]" appearing in the same file for the same type of audio problem. Rev requires "[inaudible]" in lowercase brackets. GoTranscript uses a different notation. Neither accepts a mix of styles.

Pages 1–4 are clean verbatim (fillers removed). Pages 5–8 switch to full verbatim (fillers preserved). This happens when an ASR tool applies different post-processing across transcript segments — and it fails QA because the verbatim level is supposed to be consistent throughout.

Clean verbatim by default. Speaker names in ALL CAPS followed by a colon. Timestamp format [HH:MM:SS] every 2 minutes and at speaker changes. Maximum paragraph: 8 lines. Inaudible: [inaudible]. Crosstalk: [crosstalk]. False starts and filler words removed.

Clean or full verbatim per client request. Speaker format "Speaker Name:" with title case. [inaudible] for unclear audio. No timestamp requirement by default (client can request). No strict paragraph length limit. Crosstalk marked with [crosstalk].

Strict verbatim — all fillers and false starts preserved. Timestamps required at each speaker turn. Speaker format "SPEAKER NAME:" in caps. Specific bracket format for technical notation. Paragraph breaks only at speaker changes.

Many agencies specify hybrid rules that don't map cleanly to any standard guide — for example, Rev-style speaker labels but GoTranscript-style verbatim and no timestamps. These combinations must be documented explicitly because the formatter cannot infer them.

TranscribeMe uses standard American English punctuation. Oxford comma in lists. Em dash for interruptions and abrupt stops. Ellipsis for trailing off. Question marks for direct questions. Exclamation points sparingly — only for genuinely exclamatory speech.

No. Speaker label lines end with a colon, not a period. The colon is part of the label format: [Speaker 1]: The meeting will begin shortly. The period comes at the end of the speaker's sentence, not after the label.

Non-verbal sounds are transcribed in square brackets: [laughs], [sighs], [coughs]. Include sounds when they are relevant to the conversation or emotional context. Minor background sounds are not transcribed unless they interfere with the audio or are relevant.

Transcribe profanity exactly as spoken — do not bleep, censor, or replace with asterisks unless the client specifically requests censoring in job instructions. Standard policy is verbatim profanity if clearly spoken.

TranscribeMe uses a grading system where each transcript is reviewed against the original audio. Grades factor in: word accuracy, verbatim compliance (intelligent verbatim judgments), formatting (speaker labels, paragraph structure, punctuation), and special notation accuracy. High graders access premium audio projects.

Keep "um" or "uh" when it reveals the speaker's emotional state or thought process: nervousness ("Um... I'm not sure about that"), genuine hesitation before an important statement, or processing a difficult question. Remove them when they are purely habitual and don't add meaning to the conversation.

"You know" used as a filler (e.g., "It was, you know, a really difficult decision") should be removed. "You know" that is part of the meaning (e.g., "You know what? I changed my mind.") should be kept. The test is whether removing it changes the meaning or flow of the sentence.

No. TranscribeMe explicitly prohibits using ALL CAPS for emphasis. Do not write "It was AMAZING." Use standard casing: "It was amazing." The speaker's emphasis is conveyed by transcribing the word, not by capitalizing it.

Both use a form of clean/intelligent verbatim, but TranscribeMe requires more nuance. Rev's clean verbatim is more straightforward — remove most fillers. TranscribeMe's intelligent verbatim requires you to judge each filler in context. This makes TranscribeMe transcription slower per audio minute but produces more natural-sounding output.

Repeated words are removed unless they indicate emphasis or emotion. "I, I think so" → "I think so." But "No, no, no — I completely disagree" keeps the repetition because it conveys strong disagreement. The repetition must meaningfully contribute to the speaker's communication.

Transcribio uses an AI-plus-human workflow: AI generates an initial transcript, and human reviewers correct and refine the output. Reviewers focus on correcting AI errors (homophones, proper nouns, domain-specific terms) and cleaning filler words rather than transcribing from scratch.

Priority order for Transcribio AI review: (1) proper nouns and names — most commonly wrong; (2) homophones in context (their/there, to/too); (3) technical/domain terms; (4) filler word removal; (5) punctuation corrections; (6) speaker label verification. Start with high-impact errors and work down.
Transcribio uses [Speaker N]: format — square brackets around the label, colon after closing bracket. Example: [Speaker 1]: The AI draft looks clean. [Speaker 2]: I spotted a few proper noun errors.

A single speaker must have exactly one label format from the first occurrence to the last. Mixed formats (JOHN SMITH / John / J. Smith) require a find-and-replace pass across the full document before any other formatting work.

Rev-style: timestamps every 2 minutes or at each speaker change. GoTranscript: no timestamp requirement by default. TranscribeMe: per-speaker-turn timestamps. Paragraph length limits range from 8 lines (Rev) to no limit (some custom clients).

Verify inaudible notation consistency (all [inaudible] or all [INAUDIBLE], never mixed), check bracket format for crosstalk sections, confirm verbatim level is consistent throughout, and validate that paragraph length does not exceed the client's maximum.

Clean verbatim text. Speaker names in CAPITAL LETTERS followed by a colon. Timestamps in [HH:MM:SS] format at 2-minute intervals and at speaker changes. No paragraph longer than 8 lines. Inaudible sections marked [inaudible]. False starts and fillers removed.

Optional full or clean verbatim per client request. Speaker labels in "Speaker Name:" format with consistent capitalization. [inaudible] notation for unclear audio. No timestamp requirement unless client specifies. Paragraph breaks at topic shifts rather than fixed intervals.

Structured document with consistent heading-style speaker labels, paragraph breaks, correctly formatted timestamps, and clean or full verbatim as specified. Formatted for direct delivery — no manual cleanup required before attaching to the client email.

Turn raw AI-generated transcripts into readable interview documents: speaker structure, consistent punctuation, accurate paragraph breaks, and timestamps that let readers verify context in the source recording.

Page 1: "JOHN SMITH: Thanks for joining us." Page 3: "John: So as I was saying..." Page 7: "Speaker 1: Right, exactly." — All three refer to the same speaker. Label drift of this kind fails QA at every major transcript marketplace.

[00:05:12] on page 2, (00:05:12) on page 4, [5:12] on page 6, and 00:05:12 on page 8 — all in the same document. Most style guides require a single format, and inconsistency triggers automatic rejection on automated QA systems.

"[inaudible]", "[INAUDIBLE]", "[unclear]", and "[crosstalk]" appearing in the same file for the same type of audio problem. Rev requires "[inaudible]" in lowercase brackets. GoTranscript uses a different notation. Neither accepts a mix of styles.

Pages 1–4 are clean verbatim (fillers removed). Pages 5–8 switch to full verbatim (fillers preserved). This happens when an ASR tool applies different post-processing across transcript segments — and it fails QA because the verbatim level is supposed to be consistent throughout.

Clean verbatim by default. Speaker names in ALL CAPS followed by a colon. Timestamp format [HH:MM:SS] every 2 minutes and at speaker changes. Maximum paragraph: 8 lines. Inaudible: [inaudible]. Crosstalk: [crosstalk]. False starts and filler words removed.

Clean or full verbatim per client request. Speaker format "Speaker Name:" with title case. [inaudible] for unclear audio. No timestamp requirement by default (client can request). No strict paragraph length limit. Crosstalk marked with [crosstalk].

Strict verbatim — all fillers and false starts preserved. Timestamps required at each speaker turn. Speaker format "SPEAKER NAME:" in caps. Specific bracket format for technical notation. Paragraph breaks only at speaker changes.

Many agencies specify hybrid rules that don't map cleanly to any standard guide — for example, Rev-style speaker labels but GoTranscript-style verbatim and no timestamps. These combinations must be documented explicitly because the formatter cannot infer them.

Most common AI punctuation errors in Transcribio: (1) comma splices (run-on sentences joined with commas); (2) missing terminal punctuation; (3) incorrect use of apostrophes in possessives; (4) missing question marks for interrogatives; (5) incorrect period placement in dialogue.

AI models often misidentify technical terms. As a reviewer, research correct spellings for domain-specific vocabulary. Use the job brief or client context clues. Mark uncertain terms with [?] if you cannot verify the correct spelling.

Transcribio reviewers are rated on: accuracy (word error correction rate), formatting compliance (speaker labels, paragraphs, timestamps), verbatim appropriateness (filler removal, punctuation), and review speed. Higher-rated reviewers access premium audio projects.

paragraphs: Benchmark reference for broad transcription software evaluation: median and P90 processing speed, output depth checks, and reproducible methodology by file length.

Select recordings that represent real workflow conditions: clear speech, multi-speaker with 3+ participants, recordings with background noise (HVAC, crowd, traffic), technical vocabulary, non-native accents, and fast speech above 175 WPM.

Have two independent transcriptionists produce ground-truth text for each test recording. Resolve disagreements through arbitration. Ground truth quality determines benchmark reliability — a flawed reference transcript produces meaningless WER numbers.

Upload the same recordings to each tool without pre-processing. Record wall-clock processing time from upload completion to transcript available. Use default settings unless the specific goal is to benchmark custom configurations.

Calculate WER and speaker attribution accuracy from raw output before any editing. Then time how long a single editor takes to bring each raw transcript to delivery-ready quality — same editor, same criteria, measured independently for each tool output.

Accuracy measured separately for clear speech, moderate noise (SNR 15–25dB), and heavy noise (SNR below 15dB). Results broken out by content type: interview, meeting, podcast, lecture, technical presentation — each has meaningfully different baseline accuracy.

Wall-clock time from upload completion to transcript ready, measured at 30, 60, and 120 minutes of source audio. Processing time is measured without upload duration — network speed is not a benchmark variable for the transcription engine itself.

Minutes of human editing time required to bring raw transcript to delivery quality, measured per hour of source audio. This metric captures the total operational cost better than WER alone, since a 92% accurate but unstructured transcript may require more editing than an 88% accurate but well-labeled one.
Use benchmark data across multiple audio conditions — not just the vendor's best-case scenario — before committing to a paid plan or enterprise contract. Test with your actual content type.
Run the same recordings you process weekly through each tool under consideration. Measure cleanup time, not just WER — it is the cost that your editors pay on every job.

Run controlled accuracy tests across multiple providers using a standardized test set with verified ground truth. Document audio conditions precisely — SNR level, speaker count, language, and content type — so results are reproducible.

Clear studio speech (SNR >30dB): WER typically 3–6%. Office recording with HVAC noise (SNR 20–25dB): WER typically 8–14%. Meeting room with multiple speakers sharing a single microphone (SNR <15dB): WER typically 15–25%. Vendor-published accuracy numbers rarely specify which condition they measured.

Some transcription models degrade in quality after 30–60 minutes of continuous audio — topic drift, speaker fatigue in the audio signal, and model context limits all contribute. A benchmark that only tests 10-minute clips does not reveal this degradation.

Most ASR models maintain accuracy up to approximately 160–170 WPM. Above 175 WPM — common in panel discussions, auction recordings, and some podcast styles — accuracy drops sharply. A benchmark that does not include fast-speech samples misses a common real-world failure mode.

WER counts incorrect words but does not penalize for speaker misattribution separately. A transcript that is 93% accurate on individual words but assigns 30% of dialogue to the wrong speaker will fail completely for any workflow that depends on knowing who said what.

WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / Total Reference Words. Calculated case-insensitively. Punctuation errors typically excluded. A 5% WER means 5 errors per 100 reference words — which for a 10,000-word transcript produces approximately 500 errors requiring correction.

Clear speech: single speaker, SNR above 30dB, minimal reverberation. Moderate noise: 2–4 speakers, SNR 15–25dB, background hum or traffic. Challenging: 4+ speakers on shared microphone, SNR below 15dB, overlapping speech and background noise.

Transcriptionist A produces ground truth. Transcriptionist B independently reviews and marks disagreements. Arbitration resolves disagreements using the source audio as the authoritative reference. Ground truth files are locked before any tool testing begins.

Measured separately from WER. Speaker attribution error rate = percentage of words assigned to the incorrect speaker label in the benchmark output. A separate metric from word accuracy because speaker label errors are categorically different from transcription word errors.

WER (Word Error Rate) = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / Total Reference Words. A 5% WER means approximately 5 errors per 100 words. WER is calculated against a verified ground-truth transcript, case-insensitively, typically excluding punctuation errors. It measures word-level accuracy but does not score speaker attribution errors, formatting quality, or the readability of the output — which is why WER alone is an incomplete operational benchmark.

The same human editor processes the raw output from each tool under identical conditions: same recording, same quality criteria for "delivery-ready," timed start-to-finish. The editor is not told which tool produced which output to prevent bias. Cleanup time is measured in minutes per hour of source audio. This metric captures speaker label corrections, paragraph restructuring, inaudible-section review, and verbatim level normalization — all the editing steps WER does not measure.

Most vendor-published accuracy numbers are measured on best-case audio conditions: studio-quality single-speaker speech at low noise levels. Real-world recordings — meetings, podcasts, interviews with consumer microphones — produce meaningfully lower accuracy across all tools. A vendor reporting 99% accuracy has likely measured on clean studio audio. The relevant question is accuracy at the SNR level and speaker count of your actual recordings.

It depends on the architecture. Some ASR models process audio in fixed chunks (typically 30 minutes) and reassemble independently. These models maintain consistent accuracy across length but may introduce artifacts at chunk boundaries. Other models use longer context windows that can handle topic drift better but may slow down for very long files. Testing with your actual recording duration, not just short samples, is the only reliable way to evaluate long-file behavior.

Use recordings from your actual workflow — same audio conditions, same speaker count, same content type. Do not use vendor-provided sample audio for evaluation. Measure three things: raw WER against a verified transcript, processing time per hour of audio, and cleanup time for one editor to bring the raw output to your delivery standard. The tool with the best combination of those three metrics for your content type is the right choice, regardless of marketing accuracy claims.

listItems: Word Error Rate measures how many words in the transcript differ from the ground truth — but it does not measure which errors matter. A transcript with 7% WER that misattributes 40% of speaker turns requires more editing than a 10% WER transcript where all speaker labels are correct. WER is a useful starting point, not an operational conclusion.

Benchmark audio diversity is the most commonly gamed variable in transcription accuracy claims. Testing only studio-quality clear speech (SNR above 30dB) overstates real-world accuracy by 8–15% for typical meeting, interview, and podcast content recorded with consumer-grade microphones in office environments.

Cleanup time — the number of minutes a human editor spends bringing a raw AI transcript to delivery-ready quality — is the operationally relevant metric that most transcription vendors do not publish. A tool with 94% WER that produces poorly structured output may require more editing time than an 89% WER tool that outputs clean paragraph structure with accurate speaker labels.

Broadcast rules and legal captioning requirements
Need a transcript from a video?
paragraphs: A sourced reference of 78 transcription, caption, accessibility, podcast, and speech-recognition statistics. Each number links to the original organization or study.
Written and reviewed by the VideoText editorial team . Published September 13, 2026 . Last updated September 13, 2026 .
430 million people — over 5% of the world’s population — require rehabilitation for disabling hearing loss. according to World Health Organization ( n.d. ).
WHO defines this group as people who need rehabilitation, including 34 million children.
Caveat: Disabling hearing loss is a clinical threshold, not a caption-usage survey.
Source: World Health Organization — Deafness and hearing loss (fact sheet)
The 430 million people who require rehabilitation for disabling hearing loss include 34 million children. according to World Health Organization ( n.d. ).
Child count is a subset of WHO’s disabling-hearing-loss estimate, not an additional population.
Source: World Health Organization — Deafness and hearing loss (fact sheet)
By 2050, WHO projects that nearly 2.5 billion people will have some degree of hearing loss. according to World Health Organization ( n.d. ).
This is a projection of any-degree hearing loss, not a forecast of caption or transcript demand.
Caveat: Projection, not an observed count.
Source: World Health Organization — Deafness and hearing loss (fact sheet)
By 2050, WHO estimates that more than 700 million people — about 1 in 10 — will have disabling hearing loss. according to World Health Organization ( n.d. ).
WHO presents this as the future rehabilitation caseload, not a technology-adoption forecast.
Caveat: Projection. Distinct from the 2.5 billion “any degree” figure.
Source: World Health Organization — Deafness and hearing loss (fact sheet)
Around 95.1 million children aged 5–19 years live with hearing loss worldwide. according to World Health Organization ( n.d. ).
Age-bounded child/adolescent estimate on the WHO fact sheet; it is not limited to disabling loss.
Source: World Health Organization — Deafness and hearing loss (fact sheet)
Unaddressed hearing loss poses an annual global cost of almost US$ 1 trillion, according to WHO. according to World Health Organization ( n.d. ).
WHO attributes this cost to unaddressed hearing loss. It is not a market-size figure for transcription software.
Caveat: Economic-burden estimate. Do not present it as transcription-industry revenue.
Source: World Health Organization — Deafness and hearing loss (fact sheet)
Over 1 billion young adults are at risk of permanent, avoidable hearing loss due to unsafe listening practices. according to World Health Organization ( n.d. ).
WHO frames this as a preventable-risk population, not as people who already have hearing loss.
Caveat: Risk estimate, not diagnosed prevalence.
Source: World Health Organization — Deafness and hearing loss (fact sheet)
Approximately 15% of American adults (37.5 million) ages 18 and over report some trouble hearing. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD compiles this from National Health Interview Survey analysis (Blackwell, Lucas, Clarke, 2014) and still publishes it on the official quick-statistics page (updated 20 September 2024).
Caveat: Older survey vintage than CDC NCHS Data Brief 414 (2019). Keep both; do not average them.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness

About 2 to 3 out of every 1,000 children in the United States are born with a detectable level of hearing loss in one or both ears. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD cites CDC MMWR infant-hearing identification data (1999–2007).
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness
More than 90% of deaf children are born to hearing parents. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD cites Mitchell & Karchmer (2004), Sign Language Studies.
Caveat: Foundational demographic finding; the underlying paper is from 2004.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness

1 in 8 people in the United States (13%, or 30 million) ages 12 or older has hearing loss in both ears, based on standard hearing examinations. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD cites Lin, Niparko, and Ferrucci (2011), Archives of Internal Medicine.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness

About 5% of U.S. adults ages 45–54 have disabling hearing loss; the share is 10% at ages 55–64, 22% at ages 65–74, and 55% at ages 75 and older. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD Epidemiology staff calculations from 2015–2020 NHANES using the Global Burden of Disease 35 dB better-ear threshold.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness
About 28.8 million U.S. adults could benefit from using hearing aids. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD Epidemiology estimate based on December 2015 Census Bureau noninstitutionalized population figures (personal communication, May 2016), still listed on the 2024 quick-statistics page.
Caveat: Benefit-from-aids estimate, not current hearing-aid ownership.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness

Among U.S. adults ages 70 and older with hearing loss who could benefit from hearing aids, fewer than 1 in 3 (30%) has ever used them. Among adults ages 20–69 who could benefit, about 16% have ever used them. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD combines NHIS hearing-aid-use questions with NHANES exam denominators.
Caveat: “Ever used” is not the same as current daily use.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness
Among U.S. adults ages 20–69, men are almost twice as likely as women to have hearing loss. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD cites Hoffman et al., JAMA Otolaryngology (2016).
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness

Among U.S. adults ages 20–69, the overall annual prevalence of hearing loss dropped slightly from 16% (28.0 million) in 1999–2004 to 14% (27.7 million) in 2011–2012. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
Same Hoffman et al. (2016) analysis cited by NIDCD.
Caveat: Ages 20–69 only. Not a decline in older-adult disabling loss.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness
As of July 2022, more than 1 million cochlear implants had been implanted worldwide. according to National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) ( 2024 ).
NIDCD cites Zeng (2022), JASA Express Letters. Separate U.S. FDA-registration estimates through December 2019 are 118,100 adult and 65,000 pediatric implants.
Source: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) — Quick Statistics About Hearing, Balance, & Dizziness
In 2019, 13.0% of U.S. adults aged 18 and over had some difficulty hearing even when using a hearing aid. according to National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) ( 2021 ).
NCHS Data Brief 414, based on the 2019 National Health Interview Survey question about difficulty hearing even with a hearing aid.
Caveat: Not interchangeable with NIDCD’s 15% “trouble hearing” figure; question wording differs.
Source: National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) — Hearing Difficulties Among Adults: United States, 2019 (Data Brief 414)

In 2019, 1.6% of U.S. adults aged 18 and over had a lot of difficulty hearing or could not hear at all, even when using a hearing aid. according to National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) ( 2021 ).
Same NCHS Data Brief 414 / 2019 NHIS functional-hearing question.
Source: National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) — Hearing Difficulties Among Adults: United States, 2019 (Data Brief 414)

In 2019, some difficulty hearing (even with a hearing aid) affected 6.3% of U.S. adults 18–44, 13.6% of adults 45–64, and 26.8% of adults 65 and over. according to National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) ( 2021 ).
Age gradient from NCHS Data Brief 414 Figure 1 / accompanying 508 tables.
Source: National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) — Hearing Difficulties Among Adults: United States, 2019 (Data Brief 414)

In 2019, 4.1% of U.S. adults aged 65 and over had a lot of difficulty hearing or could not hear at all, even when using a hearing aid. according to National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) ( 2021 ).
NCHS Data Brief 414 age breakout for the most severe functional category.
Source: National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) — Hearing Difficulties Among Adults: United States, 2019 (Data Brief 414)
In 2019, 7.1% of U.S. adults aged 45 and over used a hearing aid, including 8.9% of men and 5.4% of women in that age range. according to National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) ( 2021 ).
NCHS Data Brief 414 hearing-aid-use estimates for ages 45+.
Source: National Center for Health Statistics (CDC) — Hearing Difficulties Among Adults: United States, 2019 (Data Brief 414)
90% of organizations in 3Play Media’s 2024 State of Captioning survey were captioning at least some of their content — the highest share in the report’s history. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Eighth annual industry survey of 450+ respondents. 3Play is a captioning vendor; treat as a convenience sample of accessibility-interested organizations, not a census of all video publishers.
Caveat: Not a probability sample of all companies that publish video.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
33.8% of 2024 State of Captioning respondents said they caption all of their content; another 35.6% caption most of it. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Closed-captioning volume breakout (None / A little / Some / Most / All) in the 2024 report.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report

35% of 2024 State of Captioning respondents said their organization produces 500 or more hours of video content annually — the highest volume reported in the survey’s history. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Combined 501–1,000 and 1,000+ hour buckets (8.9% + 11.2% plus the report’s “35%” summary for 500+).
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
39% of respondents said they prioritize captioning by captioning everything, rather than selecting videos by legal risk, accommodations, or popularity. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Prioritization question in the closed-captioning chapter.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report

60.6% of respondents named accessibility / equal access as the primary motivator for captioning — still ahead of education, accommodations, litigation risk, and SEO. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Multiple-select motivators: educational outcomes 40.3%, accommodation requests 38%, compliance/litigation 31%, SEO/engagement 24.1%, searchability 19.1%.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
30% of organizations said budget was the biggest hurdle preventing them from closed captioning, followed by lack of resources/time (26%). according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Barrier ranking in the closed-captioning chapter. Technical challenges (12%) and uncertain organizational needs (11%) were next.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
66% of surveyed organizations said they have standards for captioning accuracy; 34% said they do not. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Policy-and-compliance chapter. The report notes that those standards are often based on WCAG or state/federal rules.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
49% of respondents said their organization has clear policies for accessibility compliance, and 41% have centralized procedures and processes. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Policy-and-compliance chapter of the 2024 survey.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
81% of respondents said they caption at least some of their social-media content. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Social-media chapter. 67% still named accessibility as the primary social-captioning motivator.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
Only 14% of respondents believed automatic captions by themselves provide an accessible experience. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Automatic-captions chapter. 27.3% start with auto captions and then edit in-house; 10.3% said they always use auto captions unedited.
Caveat: Perception of accessibility, not a measured WER study.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
27.3% of respondents said they start with automatic captions and then edit them; 23.5% said they do not use automatic captions at all. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Workflow mix also includes vendor auto-then-edit (19.8%), vendor auto only (19.1%), and always-auto (10.3%).
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
53.9% of respondents said they provide audio description at least sometimes, including 18.4% who said they provide it all the time. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Audio-description chapter. 18.8% said they do not provide AD but would like to; 27.3% said they do not.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
52.6% of respondents named video platforms — with YouTube called out as the favorite — as their main publishing destination for captioned content. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Distribution question. Learning-management systems, company websites, and social media followed.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
Almost half of respondents reported accessibility-budget increases: 28% said the budget increased moderately and 20% said it increased significantly. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
40.8% of respondents satisfy media-accessibility needs with a mix of in-house work and vendors — still the most common model, but down 15% from the previous year. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
The report says using several vendors rose by almost the same amount. Quality/expertise (45%) was the top reason to use a vendor.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report

U.S. video programming distributors and programmers must closed-caption 100% of new, nonexempt English- and Spanish-language video programming on each channel each calendar quarter. according to Federal Communications Commission / U.S. eCFR ( n.d. ).
This is a legal requirement in 47 C.F.R. § 79.1, not an observed compliance rate. Exemptions and economically burdensome waivers exist.
Caveat: Requirement ≠ measured compliance. Do not quote this as “100% of U.S. TV is captioned.”
Source: Federal Communications Commission / U.S. eCFR — 47 CFR § 79.1 — Closed captioning of televised video programming

U.S. distributors and programmers must closed-caption 75% of pre-rule, nonexempt English- and Spanish-language video programming each calendar quarter. according to Federal Communications Commission / U.S. eCFR ( n.d. ).
Companion obligation in 47 C.F.R. § 79.1 for programming that predates the captioning rules.
Source: Federal Communications Commission / U.S. eCFR — 47 CFR § 79.1 — Closed captioning of televised video programming
As of 2024, 85% of U.S. adults said they ever use YouTube — more than any other online platform Pew asked about that year. according to Pew Research Center ( 2025 ).
Pew social-media fact sheet row dated 10 June 2024, restated in “5 facts about Americans and YouTube” (28 February 2025). Facebook was 70% in the same 2024 wave.
Source: Pew Research Center — 5 facts about Americans and YouTube
In Pew’s 5 February–18 June 2025 National Public Opinion Reference Survey of 5,022 U.S. adults, 84% said they use YouTube. according to Pew Research Center ( 2025 ).
Address-based NPORS sample conducted by SSRS (web, mail, and phone). Age breakouts: 95% of ages 18–29, 92% of 30–49, 85% of 50–64, and 64% of 65+.
Source: Pew Research Center — Social Media Fact Sheet
90% of U.S. teens ages 13–17 said they use YouTube in Pew’s 18 September–10 October 2024 teen survey, down slightly from 95% in 2022. according to Pew Research Center ( 2024 ).
YouTube remained the most widely used platform asked about. 73% of teens said they use YouTube daily, including 15% “almost constantly.”
Source: Pew Research Center — Teens, Social Media and Technology 2024
73% of U.S. teens said they go on YouTube daily, the highest daily-use rate among platforms Pew asked about in 2024. according to Pew Research Center ( 2024 ).
Same 2024 teen survey. 96% of teens reported using the internet daily.
Source: Pew Research Center — Teens, Social Media and Technology 2024
70% of U.S. adults said they use Facebook in Pew’s 10 June 2024 social-media fact-sheet wave — second to YouTube’s 85%. according to Pew Research Center ( 2024 ).
Included because Facebook remains a major distribution surface for captioned social video in the 3Play survey, not because Facebook published a silent-video statistic.
Source: Pew Research Center — Social Media Fact Sheet
50% of U.S. adults said they use Instagram in the same 10 June 2024 Pew wave. according to Pew Research Center ( 2024 ).
Instagram is one of the social surfaces where 3Play respondents most often publish captioned video.
Source: Pew Research Center — Social Media Fact Sheet
51% of Americans age 12+ have watched a podcast. according to Edison Research ( 2025 ).
Video-podcast reach from Infinite Dial 2025. 48% have both listened and watched.
Source: Edison Research — The Infinite Dial 2025
73% of Americans age 12+ have consumed a podcast in audio or video form, about 210 million people. according to Edison Research ( 2025 ).
Combined listen-or-watch lifetime reach. Edison’s Podcast Consumer 2025 restates the same Infinite Dial figures.
Source: Edison Research — The Infinite Dial 2025 / The Podcast Consumer 2025
55% of Americans age 12+ are monthly podcast consumers, about 158 million people — an all-time high. according to Edison Research ( 2025 ).
Monthly listen-or-watch. Edison notes this is a record.
Source: Edison Research — The Podcast Consumer 2025
40% of Americans age 12+ consumed a podcast in the last week, about 115 million people. according to Edison Research ( 2025 ).
Weekly listen-or-watch, also described as an all-time high.
Source: Edison Research — The Podcast Consumer 2025
Americans ages 13+ spent 773 million hours per week with podcasts in 2025, a 355% increase from 170 million weekly hours in 2015. according to Edison Research ( 2025 ).
Edison Share of Ear, restated in The Podcast Consumer 2025. This is time spent, not episode count.
Source: Edison Research — The Podcast Consumer 2025 (Share of Ear)
37% of the U.S. population age 12+ watched a video podcast in the last month, and 26% watched one in the last week. according to Edison Research ( 2025 ).
Podcast Consumer 2025 video-podcast breakout. Edison notes video-podcast watchers are younger and more diverse than audio-only listeners.
Source: Edison Research — The Podcast Consumer 2025

The Whisper speech models were trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask supervision collected from audio transcripts on the internet. according to OpenAI (Radford, Kim, Xu, Brockman, McLeavey, Sutskever) ( 2022 ).
Radford et al., “Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision” (arXiv:2212.04356). This is training-data scale, not a user-adoption statistic.
Source: OpenAI (Radford, Kim, Xu, Brockman, McLeavey, Sutskever) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
After the paper’s text normalizer, Whisper Large V2 scored 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech Clean — matching wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM) at 2.7%. according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
Table 2 of the Whisper paper. Relative error reduction vs wav2vec on that row is 0.0%.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
Whisper Large V2 scored 5.2% WER on LibriSpeech Other, versus 6.2% for wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM). according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
Table 2. “Other” is the harder LibriSpeech split.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision

Whisper Large V2 scored 25.5% WER on CHiME-6, versus 65.8% for wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM) — a 61.2% relative error reduction on that noisy conversational set. according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
Table 2. Illustrates why a single “AI is 97% accurate” claim is misleading: the same model’s WER jumps on dinner-party/CHiME audio.
Caveat: High WER; not comparable to LibriSpeech clean.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
Whisper Large V2 scored 9.0% WER on Common Voice, versus 29.9% for wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM). according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
Table 2. Common Voice is crowd-recorded, more accent- and domain-diverse than LibriSpeech clean.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
Whisper Large V2 scored 16.9% WER on AMI IHM (headset meeting speech) and 36.4% WER on AMI SDM1 (single distant microphone). according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
Table 2. Distant-microphone meeting audio more than doubles WER versus headset audio in this comparison.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
Whisper Large V2 scored 17.6% WER on CallHome and 13.8% WER on Switchboard. according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
Table 2 telephone-conversation rows. These are the closest published Whisper-paper proxies for spontaneous two-party speech.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
Whisper Large V2 scored 4.0% WER on TED-LIUM, versus 10.5% for wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM). according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
Table 2. Prepared talks, closer to lecture/podcast monologue than to overlapping meetings.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision

Across the Table 2 evaluation sets, Whisper Large V2 averaged 12.8% WER versus 29.3% for wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM), a 55.2% average relative error reduction. according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
The paper’s robustness headline. Do not quote 12.8% as “Whisper accuracy in production captioning.”
Caveat: Average of research sets, not a traffic-weighted industry WER.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
Even the smallest zero-shot Whisper model (39 million parameters) had a 6.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. according to OpenAI (Radford et al.) ( 2022 ).
The authors use this to argue that robustness, not LibriSpeech clean WER, is the interesting axis.
Source: OpenAI (Radford et al.) — Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
LibriSpeech is a corpus of approximately 1,000 hours of 16 kHz read English speech derived from LibriVox audiobooks. according to OpenSLR / Panayotov et al. ( 2015 ).
Panayotov, Chen, Povey, and Khudanpur, ICASSP 2015. Official distribution: OpenSLR 12. Training is split into ~100 / 360 / 500 hour subsets plus clean/other dev and test sets.
Source: OpenSLR / Panayotov et al. — LibriSpeech ASR corpus

Mozilla Common Voice 20 (11 December 2024) contains 33,150 hours of speech, of which 22,108 hours were community-validated, across 133 languages in the scripted-speech dataset. according to Mozilla Foundation (Common Voice) ( 2024 ).
Official Mozilla Foundation release note. The release added 566 new hours and 515 newly validated hours, plus four new languages.
Source: Mozilla Foundation (Common Voice) — Common Voice 20 is Now Available

In 2022–23, 7.5 million U.S. students ages 3–21 received special education and/or related services under IDEA — 15% of public-school students. according to National Center for Education Statistics ( 2024 ).
NCES Condition of Education indicator on students with disabilities. Caption/transcript obligations in schools sit against this population, not only the hearing-impairment subcategory.
Source: National Center for Education Statistics — Students With Disabilities (Condition of Education)

Students with hearing impairments accounted for 0.9% of students ages 3–21 served under IDEA in 2022–23 (69,595 students). according to National Center for Education Statistics / Office of Special Education Programs ( 2023 ).
NCES Digest tables 204.30 and 204.50. The Condition of Education narrative groups hearing impairment with several low-incidence categories at “2 percent or less.”
Source: National Center for Education Statistics / Office of Special Education Programs — Digest of Education Statistics, Table 204.50 (2022–23)

Among students ages 14–21 served under IDEA who exited school in 2021–22, 84% of students with hearing impairments graduated with a regular high school diploma — the highest graduation share among disability types NCES reported. according to National Center for Education Statistics ( 2024 ).
NCES Condition of Education. The lowest regular-diploma share in the same comparison was 40% for students with multiple disabilities.
Source: National Center for Education Statistics — Students With Disabilities (Condition of Education)

National data cited by the National Deaf Center show that 4.9% of deaf adults are currently enrolled in postsecondary institutions, compared with 10.0% of hearing people. according to National Deaf Center on Postsecondary Outcomes (University of Texas at Austin) ( 2023 ).
NDC undergraduate-enrollment brief citing Bloom, Palmer, and Winninghoff (2023), using NPSAS and related national sources.
Caveat: NDC analysis of federal survey data; “deaf” includes people who report being deaf or having serious difficulty hearing.
Source: National Deaf Center on Postsecondary Outcomes (University of Texas at Austin) — Undergraduate Enrollment of Deaf Students in the United States (2019–2020)

In National Deaf Center / SRI research on young deaf adults, 87% of college graduates were employed compared with 68% of high-school graduates. according to National Deaf Center on Postsecondary Outcomes ( 2022 ).
Palmer, Davidson, Cawthon, and Newman analysis summarized by NDC. Wages were about 33% higher for college graduates than for high-school graduates in the same comparison.
Caveat: Employment gap associated with education; not a caption-usage finding.
Source: National Deaf Center on Postsecondary Outcomes — College Matters: New Research Shows Better Outcomes for Deaf People Who Continue Their Education
78% of respondents said they are streaming live video content. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Live-captions chapter. Zoom was the most-mentioned live platform, followed by YouTube and Facebook.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
Among live-video respondents, 33% said they live-caption all the time and 46% said they live-caption sometimes. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Live-captions chapter. Automatic live tools were the most-used method (33.1%), ahead of CART/human captioners (27.6%).
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report
Among respondents who use live automatic captioning tools, 55% reported inaccuracy and errors as their biggest challenge. according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
The same chapter says automatic solutions are the most popular live method (33.1%) even though popularity “doesn’t equal perfection.”
Caveat: Self-reported challenge, not a scored WER.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report

61.6% of respondents who localize content said they use subtitling — the most common localization method in the 2024 survey, ahead of non-English captions (40.4%), live translation (27.3%), and dubbing (25.3%). according to 3Play Media ( 2024 ).
Localization chapter. 22% localize all the time and 38% localize sometimes (60% at least sometimes). The report notes a 17% increase in organizations localizing at least some content.
Caveat: Sample skews to U.S. higher education, which the report itself says likely favors subtitles over dubbing.
Source: 3Play Media — 2024 State of Captioning Report

Upload the video or paste a public URL. Word-level timestamp alignment produces more accurate line breaks than sentence-level alignment — each subtitle break falls at a natural pause rather than a word boundary mid-phrase.

Flag any line above 17 CPS and split it. An 8-word subtitle in a 1.2-second window hits approximately 24 CPS — unreadable for most viewers. Merge subtitle lines shorter than 0.8 seconds, which display too briefly to register.

Subtitle overlap — where the next block starts before the previous one ends — causes display flicker in most players. Any gap shorter than 0.1 seconds between adjacent subtitles should be merged or widened to prevent rendering artifacts.

Export SRT for YouTube, Vimeo, and video editors. Export VTT for HTML5 web players and streaming platforms that support caption positioning. Choose burned-caption output for Instagram Reels, TikTok clips, and any social context where autoplay without sound is expected.

Standard timed subtitle format: sequence number, timestamp pair (00:00:00,000 → 00:00:00,000 with comma separator), and one or two lines of caption text per block. Supported by YouTube, Vimeo, LinkedIn, most video editors, and accessibility workflows.

WebVTT format with period timestamp separators (00:00:00.000 → 00:00:00.000). Used by HTML5 video players, streaming services, and accessibility platforms. Unlike SRT, VTT supports <cue> positioning metadata, text styling, and karaoke-mode highlighting.

Permanently embedded caption text rendered directly into the video frame — cannot be toggled off by the viewer. Required for platforms that strip external caption tracks. Font rendering, shadow depth, and vertical position all need QA review after encoding because video compression can degrade caption legibility.
Generate SRT for YouTube upload, export burned captions for Instagram Reels, and produce VTT for course platform embeds — all from the same subtitle pass without reformatting timing.
Produce synchronized captions that meet WCAG 2.1 timing and reading-speed requirements. CPS validation catches lines that fail accessibility guidelines before the video goes live.
Export SRT or VTT for import into Premiere, DaVinci Resolve, or Final Cut Pro. Accurate word-level timestamps eliminate the need to manually re-sync caption timing after import.

Eight words spoken in 1.2 seconds: "we need to fix this before the deadline" at 24 CPS. The line must be split into two display segments within the same timing window to hit the readable 14–17 CPS range.
Block ending at 00:01:23,500 overlapping a block starting at 00:01:23,200 causes display flicker and rendering failure in most SRT players. A subtitle validator catches this before upload.

A two-line subtitle with 44+ characters per line at default font sizes clips at the bottom of mobile video frames. The safe area for mobile subtitles is a single line, 38 characters maximum, positioned at 85% vertical height.

Font stroke weight, drop shadow depth, and subtitle vertical position all shift slightly after H.264 encoding. Captions that look correct in preview may become harder to read in the encoded file — requires a post-encode QA pass before publishing.

UTF-8 encoding required. Maximum 1,500 subtitle blocks per file. Timestamp format: 00:00:00,000 (comma separator, not period). Files over 1,500 blocks need splitting before upload. YouTube auto-syncs uploaded SRT to audio — small timing offsets are corrected automatically.

TikTok generates its own auto-captions and displays them over uploaded SRT files in most cases. Burned captions are the reliable method for ensuring accurate captions appear on TikTok content. SRT upload works but TikTok may override it.

Instagram does not display soft subtitle tracks during autoplay in Feed or Reels. Burned captions are the only reliable method for ensuring captions appear for silent autoplay viewers. Instagram's built-in auto-caption feature can also be used after upload, but accuracy varies.

VTT uses period timestamp separators (00:00:00.000) while SRT uses commas (00:00:00,000). Swapping the separator character breaks parsing in most players. VTT files must begin with the WEBVTT header line — SRT files must not.

CPS stands for characters per second — how fast the viewer must read a subtitle line before it disappears. The readable range is 14–17 CPS for most general audiences. Above 21 CPS, a significant percentage of viewers cannot finish reading the line before it vanishes, even if the text is accurate. Most automated subtitle tools generate lines without a CPS check, which is why reviewing reading speed is part of subtitle QA before any platform upload.

Instagram Reels does not display soft subtitle tracks during autoplay in Feed. External SRT or VTT files uploaded to Instagram are not surfaced for most viewers. For Reels content, burned (hardcoded) captions are the only reliable method for ensuring captions appear — either by using a burn workflow before upload or using Instagram's built-in auto-caption feature after upload, which has variable accuracy.

Video encoding (particularly H.264 and H.265) applies compression that slightly degrades text edges. Font stroke weight, drop shadow contrast, and subtitle position all shift after encoding. Captions that look clean in an editing preview may develop legibility issues in the exported file. A post-encode QA pass — watching 2–3 minutes of the encoded video at actual playback size — should be part of any burned caption workflow before the file is published.

SRT uses comma separators in timestamps: 00:01:23,456 → 00:01:25,123. VTT uses period separators: 00:01:23.456 → 00:01:25.123. Swapping the separator character causes parsing failures in most players — the file appears empty or throws an error. SRT files must not begin with a header; VTT files must begin with the line "WEBVTT". The two formats are otherwise structurally similar but not interchangeable.

Progressive timing drift — where captions start slightly late early in the video and progressively fall further behind — usually indicates an audio-video sync issue in the source file, not a transcription error. The subtitle timestamps were generated against audio that does not match the video track timing. Fix: use the subtitle timing fixer to shift all timestamps by the measured offset at a known sync point early in the video. If the drift accelerates over time, the source file has a variable frame rate issue that requires frame-rate normalization before re-captioning.

VideoText exports SRT and VTT subtitle files. SRT works with YouTube, Vimeo, LinkedIn, and most video editors. VTT is the standard for HTML5 web players and streaming platforms — it also supports styling and positioning metadata that SRT does not carry. Burned caption output is available for social clips that require permanently embedded text. All exports are UTF-8 encoded.

Burned captions create a permanent workflow commitment — any timing correction or text fix after encoding requires re-encoding the full video. For long-form content this is hours of lost render time, which is why burn decisions need to happen after QA, not before.

Platform subtitle requirements are not interchangeable: TikTok displays a 2-line maximum with specific font rendering; YouTube accepts up to 1,500 SRT blocks and requires UTF-8 encoding; Instagram Reels ignores soft subtitle tracks on autoplay entirely, making burned captions the only reliable option for Reels.

Trint is built for newsrooms and media teams that need collaborative transcript editing, search across transcripts, and integrations with publishing workflows. If your team edits transcripts together and publishes to CMS — Trint is built for that.

Full transcript with speaker labels, AI summary, chapter timestamps, and SRT subtitle file — all from one upload. Ready to publish in under 5 minutes. No team editing features, but for individual creators and small teams, the free tier covers the full workflow.

VideoText: Upload video → get SRT → translate to 70+ languages → burn into video. Four tools, one platform, free to start. Trint: Upload → transcript → export SRT → use separate tool for translation → use separate tool for burning. More steps, more cost.

VideoText covers transcript + SRT + translate + burn in one platform. Upload MP4/MOV and publish in under 5 minutes.
